title: The Human Is an Async API — Melanie Warrick, Temporal
talk_summary: A Temporal engineer demos multi-agent ice-cream delivery orchestration where human-in-the-loop input is modeled as a durable wait-condition plus signal rather than a blocking call, so the rest of the system keeps running and state survives worker crashes. The core transferable idea is durable execution: workflows (deterministic step tracking) and activities (non-deterministic model/tool calls) with parked, replayable state.

takeaways.technique: Durable wait-condition + signal for human/async gates
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of a blocking call to a human, they isolate the event, park the workflow with a wait condition, and inject the human's answer later via a signal; other workflows keep running and state is persisted externally.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You want a wait condition and a signal. You're allowing yourself to isolate an event, apply a wait condition, store that in that workflow

takeaways.technique: Replay from event log on restart
takeaways.what_they_do: When the worker is killed and restarted, the event log is replayed up to the last checkpoint so the workflow resumes at the correct next step instead of redoing work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your event log is getting replayed. It's not redone. It's just replayed up until the point at which it last left off

takeaways.technique: Separate deterministic steps from non-deterministic calls
takeaways.what_they_do: Workflow code is deterministic step-tracking; every model call and tool call is wrapped as a non-deterministic activity, giving a clean boundary for retries and state.
takeaways.evidence_quote: workflows are deterministic, activities are non-deterministic

takeaways.what_they_do: Built-in timeout primitives bound how long a workflow waits on a human before taking another path.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you're waiting on a human to respond and you want to make sure that it only waits for so long, you can apply timeouts

takeaways.what_they_do: Decide when a human must be in the loop by weighing the cost of being wrong against alert fatigue from over-asking.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the cost of being wrong is high ... alert fatigue is real ... you just start saying yes, yes, yes
